issues.description: The title/abstract/introduction repeatedly frame the study as using a national probability/general population sample, but the Methods state that participants were recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool. These are fundamentally different sampling frames. This affects interpretation, external validity, and the rationale contrasting student versus general-population samples.
issues.quote: “We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years.” / “We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington.”

issues.description: The manuscript claims the results are highly generalisable because the sample is nationally representative, yet the reported sample is small, young, mostly female, mostly Pākehā, and recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool. This is not nationally representative of New Zealand adults and makes population-level generalizations inappropriate.
issues.quote: “Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.”

issues.subcategory: sample size inconsistent with reported precision
issues.description: The Methods report N = 374, but Table 1 reports extremely narrow confidence intervals for correlations, means, and SDs that are implausible for N = 374. For example, r = .21 with 95% CI [.18, .23] would require a much larger sample. This suggests either the N, the table, or the analytic sample is wrong, undermining confidence in all reported estimates.
issues.quote: “Of the 374 participants included in this study...” / “RWA | .21*** [.18, .23]”

issues.subcategory: participant demographics inconsistent with general population
issues.description: The sample has a Time 1 mean age of 19.42 years and 68% female, which is consistent with a psychology student sample, not the stated national probability sample. This contradicts the study’s core framing and the discussion’s interpretation as general population evidence.
issues.quote: “the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.”

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between describing the outcome as environmentalism, environmental concern, willingness to sacrifice, willingness to change behaviour, and willingness to make sacrifices, but the Methods list only two concern/exaggeration items and do not include a sacrifice or behavioral-change item. The operationalization does not consistently match the construct being interpreted.
issues.quote: “Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, ‘How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?’ and ‘To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?’”

issues.description: The Data Analysis says the model examines “willingness to sacrifice for the environment,” while the Measures section says environmentalism was measured as concern about environmental problems. The table labels the variable WILL. This inconsistency obscures what construct was actually analyzed.
issues.quote: “We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.”

issues.description: Environmentalism is represented by only two items, one of which assesses perceived exaggeration and likely requires reverse-coding. The manuscript does not report whether the item was reverse-coded, whether the two items formed an acceptable scale at each time point, or whether this two-item composite validly captures broad environmentalism or willingness to sacrifice.
issues.quote: “‘How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?’ and ‘To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?’”

issues.description: The manuscript does not specify how SDO, RWA, or environmentalism composites were scored, how reverse-coded items were handled, whether items were averaged or modeled latently, or whether higher scores consistently indicate higher SDO/RWA/environmentalism. This limits replicability and interpretation of coefficients.
issues.quote: “Participants rated the extent to which they agreed with each item on 7-point Likert scales...”

issues.description: The RWA measure differs across waves because one item was omitted at Time 2 but included elsewhere. This can create artificial longitudinal change or bias cross-lagged estimates unless measurement invariance or harmonized scoring is demonstrated. The manuscript does not report how this was handled.
issues.quote: “The item ... was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.”

issues.description: The manuscript directs readers to a website for procedure, retention, and demographics rather than reporting the necessary information. For a five-wave longitudinal study, wave-specific Ns, retention rates, attrition patterns, and missingness mechanisms are essential to evaluate validity.
issues.quote: “Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.”

issues.description: Analyses used listwise deletion across five waves. In longitudinal studies this can substantially reduce N and bias estimates if missingness is not completely at random. The manuscript does not report the amount of missing data, the final analytic N after deletion, comparisons of retained versus dropped participants, or justification for listwise deletion instead of FIML/multiple imputation.
issues.quote: “Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.”

issues.description: The study uses five measurement points, but no wave-specific Ns are reported. Without knowing how many participants contributed data at each time point and how many remained in the listwise-deleted sample, readers cannot evaluate statistical power, attrition bias, or the meaning of the reported estimates.
issues.quote: “This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).”

issues.description: The manuscript describes the study as spanning five years, but the Methods state participants were surveyed across five semesters from 2009 to 2013. Five semesters is approximately 2.5 academic years, not five years, while 2009 to 2013 could be five calendar years depending on timing. The timing and lag structure are unclear.
issues.quote: “across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)”

issues.description: Cross-lagged estimates depend on the time interval between waves, yet the manuscript does not specify when each wave occurred or whether intervals were equal. This is especially problematic because a stationary model assumes comparable lag effects across intervals.
issues.quote: “across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013)”

issues.description: The authors impose time-invariant cross-lagged parameters and residual variances because of substantive interest, but do not report tests comparing constrained and unconstrained models. If effects vary across time, stationarity constraints can bias estimates and obscure meaningful developmental or contextual changes.
issues.quote: “We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.”

issues.description: The Data Analysis section states twice that cross-lagged associations were constrained to equality. This appears to be an editing error and raises ambiguity about the actual sequence of model constraints.
issues.quote: “We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.”

issues.description: The analysis describes constraining item residual variances, implying a latent-variable model, but Results and Table 1 describe scale reliabilities and variable-level correlations, and no measurement model, factor loadings, or invariance tests are reported. It is unclear whether the cross-lagged model used observed composites or latent variables.
issues.quote: “We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.”

issues.description: Longitudinal comparisons and cross-lagged paths among latent constructs require at least some evidence of measurement invariance across waves. This is especially important given shortened scales and a missing RWA item at Time 2. No configural, metric, scalar, or residual invariance tests are reported.
issues.quote: “The model included three variables across five measurement points...”

issues.description: The manuscript reports “SD” for regression/path coefficients where standard errors are intended. This is a reporting error that can confuse interpretation and replication.
issues.quote: “SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001...)”

issues.description: The reported RMSEA point estimate is .03 but the 90% CI is [.025, .026], which does not contain the rounded point estimate unless rounding is highly misleading. This suggests a reporting or calculation error.

The model has CFI = .86, which is generally below conventional thresholds for acceptable fit, and an enormous significant chi-square. The authors accept the model based on RMSEA/SRMR while dismissing indices affected by complexity. Poor comparative fit may indicate misspecification, especially in a constrained longitudinal model.
issues.quote: “Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit... therefore the model was accepted.”

issues.description: Several chi-square difference tests are reported as “2(1)” rather than χ²(1), and one lacks a statistic symbol entirely. This is a reporting problem, and in one case the value is implausibly enormous relative to the compared coefficients.
issues.quote: “We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126”

issues.subcategory: incorrect conclusion from nonsignificant difference test
issues.description: The authors test whether SDO and RWA differ in predictive strength and find the equality-constrained model does not fit significantly worse, χ²(1)=2.34, p=.126. This means they do not have statistical evidence that SDO is stronger than RWA, yet they still interpret SDO as stronger based on coefficient magnitudes.
issues.quote: “We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor...”

issues.description: The Discussion states that SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA, but the Results report a nonsignificant comparison of those paths. This overstates the evidence and contradicts the reported test.
issues.quote: “In this context, both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA.”

issues.description: The reported estimate for environmentalism predicting SDO is B = -.04 with 95% CI [-.04, -.03]. The point estimate lies on the boundary of the interval and, with SD/SE = .002, the interval would be expected to be approximately [-.044, -.036]. Rounding may explain this, but the reporting is imprecise and potentially misleading.

The reported difference test for lagged effects between SDO and RWA is χ²(1)=15,389.13, which is extraordinarily large and implausible given the coefficient magnitudes and reported N=374. This likely reflects a reporting or computational error.
issues.quote: “These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)”

issues.description: The Methods state p < .05 was adopted, but the Figure caption says all paths meet p < .01 unless otherwise noted. Table notes use p < .001. The manuscript does not consistently define or apply alpha thresholds.
issues.quote: “we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05” / “All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.”

issues.subcategory: large sample justification inconsistent with N
issues.description: The authors justify a significance threshold with “large sample size,” but the Methods report only 374 participants. If the true sample is 374, it is not unusually large for complex longitudinal SEM with many parameters; if much larger, the Methods N is wrong.
issues.quote: “Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05...”

issues.description: If the reported N=374 is correct, the model is highly complex, with three constructs across five waves and item-level residual constraints, producing df=2279. Such a model may be underpowered or unstable for estimating numerous latent parameters, particularly with listwise deletion and shortened scales. No power or sensitivity analysis is provided.
issues.quote: “Of the 374 participants included in this study...” / “χ2(2279) = 36511.73”

issues.description: The paper references Figure 1 for autoregressive and cross-lagged paths, but the manuscript text does not provide the complete set of coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, and residual correlations. Without full results, readers cannot assess the model.
issues.quote: “As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time...”

issues.description: The Figure caption is provided but not the actual figure or numerical path estimates for all autoregressive and cross-lagged effects. Key evidence for the conclusions is therefore missing from the manuscript as presented.
issues.quote: “Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL).”

issues.subcategory: causal claims from observational cross-lagged data
issues.description: The study is observational and survey-based. Cross-lagged associations can establish temporal ordering conditional on model assumptions but do not rule out time-varying confounding, stable unmeasured traits, measurement artifacts, or reverse/reciprocal causation. The manuscript nevertheless makes strong causal claims.
issues.quote: “These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.”

issues.description: Traditional cross-lagged panel models confound within-person change with between-person stable differences unless random-intercept or other trait-stable models are used. The manuscript interprets cross-lagged coefficients as changes and causal influence without addressing this limitation.
issues.quote: “SDO has a stonger influence on environmental attitudes over time than the reverse.”

issues.description: No covariates or alternative explanations are included in the model, despite likely confounders such as political orientation, socioeconomic status, education, gender, age, personality, religiosity, and cohort/contextual changes. The Discussion acknowledges possible third variables only after making causal claims.
issues.quote: “Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable.”

issues.description: The manuscript concludes that motivation to exploit the environment comes from dominance and authority/tradition, but no direct measures of motivation to exploit, dominance over nature, perceived hierarchy threat, tradition, or authority submission mechanisms are analyzed. The causal-mechanistic interpretation exceeds the data.
issues.quote: “The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to authority.”

issues.description: The paper interprets RWA effects as desire to submit to authority and tradition, but the six-item RWA scale likely mixes authoritarian submission, aggression, and conventionalism, and the analysis treats it as unidimensional. This is problematic given the Introduction cites evidence that RWA dimensions have differential associations with pro-environmental attitudes.
issues.quote: “Reese [20] found that the dimensions of RWA differentially predict pro-environmental attitudes: authoritarian submission predicts greater pro-environmentalism, authoritarian aggression predicts lower pro-environmentalism...”

issues.description: The SDO scale includes dominance and equality/anti-egalitarianism items, but the analysis treats SDO as unidimensional. Prior work cited by the manuscript shows SDO dimensions may differentially predict environmentalism. Collapsing dimensions can obscure construct-specific pathways.
issues.quote: “Three items favoured dominance... and three favoured equality...”

issues.description: Only examples of SDO and RWA items are given, not all six items. Because shortened scales may have lower reliability and different content coverage, full item reporting is needed for replication and construct evaluation.
issues.quote: “Social dominance orientation was assessed using six items from Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] SDO6 scale.”

issues.description: The authors acknowledge SDO and RWA reliabilities are poorer than full scales, with alpha around .69-.70 at Time 1. Low reliability attenuates associations, can bias structural paths in observed-variable models, and raises concerns about measurement precision over time. Reliabilities for all waves are not reported.
issues.quote: “Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used...”

issues.description: Table 1 appears to report internal consistencies on the diagonal only at Time 1. For a five-wave longitudinal analysis, reliability should be reported for each construct at each wave, especially because item content changed for RWA at Time 2.
issues.quote: “Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.”

issues.description: The table note says confidence intervals are based on “1000 iterations,” but does not specify whether these are bootstrap resamples, Monte Carlo iterations, or something else. For correlations, means, and SDs, the method for CIs should be clear and reproducible.
issues.quote: “Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations.”

issues.description: The authors infer one correlation is stronger because confidence intervals do not overlap. Non-overlap is a conservative and indirect approach; a formal test comparing dependent correlations sharing a variable would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: “the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval.”

issues.description: The manuscript does not report preregistration, a priori hypotheses, planned constraints, inclusion/exclusion decisions, or handling of alternative models. Given multiple possible longitudinal specifications, scale constructions, and constraints, undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom are a concern.
issues.quote: “A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.”

issues.subcategory: syntax not available at review stage
issues.description: The manuscript says syntax will be available only upon acceptance. For peer review and reproducibility, the syntax or enough model specification detail should be available at submission, especially for a complex constrained SEM.
issues.quote: “A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.”

issues.subcategory: lack of controls for survey design/weights
issues.description: If the study truly used a national probability sample/NZAVS data, the analysis should describe sampling weights, clustering/stratification, and procedures for restoring representativeness. If it used a student sample, national probability claims are false. In either case, survey design handling is missing.
issues.quote: “using a large, national probability sample...”

issues.description: The Methods provide almost no procedural details: recruitment process, consent, compensation, survey mode, timing of measures, ethics approval, and whether the same participants were tracked are not adequately described. Referring readers to a website is insufficient for replication.
issues.quote: “Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.”

issues.description: All constructs are self-reported in the same survey context using Likert scales, which may inflate associations through common method variance, acquiescence, social desirability, or response style. The manuscript does not address this limitation.
issues.quote: “Again, responses were on a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).”

issues.description: The study measures self-reported attitudes/concern but repeatedly makes claims about willingness to change behaviour and pro-environmental action. Attitudinal responses do not necessarily reflect actual behavioral change or sacrifice.
issues.quote: “people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment”

issues.subcategory: climate change extrapolation from general environmental items
issues.description: The Introduction and Discussion emphasize climate change denial and climate mitigation, but the measured outcome concerns the current state of the natural environment and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems generally. The construct does not specifically assess climate change beliefs, denial, mitigation behavior, or climate policy support.
issues.quote: “Research on the psychological foundations of climate change denial...” / “Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems.”

issues.description: Even if the sample were representative of New Zealand, the authors sometimes generalize to “people” and “the general population” broadly. Ideology-environment relations may vary across political and cultural contexts, which the manuscript itself notes for SDO-RWA associations.
issues.quote: “The take home message from our study is that for those in the general population...”

issues.description: The authors infer from a cross-lagged path that New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism more than social dominance. This broad sociopolitical/socialization claim is not directly tested and is especially untenable if the sample is students rather than nationally representative.
issues.quote: “this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.”

issues.description: The authors predicted reciprocal cross-time effects between SDO and RWA but found only RWA predicted SDO. The Discussion then states this is consistent with Duckitt et al., but the earlier Current Study framed reciprocal effects as expected from Duckitt. The theoretical rationale is applied inconsistently.
issues.quote: “we expect reciprocal cross-time effects.” / “This contradicted our initial expectations, however it is consistent with Duckitt et al. [23]...”

issues.description: The Methods say standardized parameters are presented, but the Results and Figure caption report unstandardized parameters. This matters because comparisons of path strength across constructs depend on whether coefficients are standardized or unstandardized.
issues.quote: “We present standardized parameters...” / “Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters...”

issues.description: The authors compare unstandardized coefficients from SDO and RWA to environmentalism to conclude one is stronger. Because SDO and RWA have different variances and scale properties, unstandardized coefficients are not directly comparable as effect sizes unless predictors are on equivalent metrics or standardized effects are used.
issues.quote: “based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor...”

issues.description: The authors state that a traditional Wald test is not possible because of constraints in the model, but equality constraints and Wald tests are standard in SEM. They do not explain why Wald testing was impossible, raising concerns about statistical understanding or reporting.
issues.quote: “Due to the nature of the analysis and the constraints placed on the model, the traditional Wald test to confirm that SDO is a statistically stronger predictor than RWA is not possible.”

issues.subcategory: estimator and missing-data assumptions not reported
issues.description: The SEM estimator, treatment of Likert indicators as continuous/categorical, standard error type, and convergence information are not reported. These choices materially affect estimates, fit indices, and inference.
issues.quote: “The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29]).”

issues.description: All measures use 7-point Likert responses, but the analysis does not state whether items were treated as continuous or ordinal and which estimator was used. This is particularly important for item-level latent modeling.
issues.quote: “Participants responded on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much)”

issues.subcategory: reference to WILL not aligned with Methods
issues.description: Table 1 notes WILL as willingness to make sacrifices, but the Methods environmental items do not ask about willingness to sacrifice. This suggests either the wrong items are reported or the wrong label is used.
issues.quote: “WILL = willingness to make sacrifices for the environment.”

issues.description: Only Time 1 descriptives and correlations are provided, despite five waves. Longitudinal studies should report means, SDs, reliabilities, and correlations across all waves to evaluate stability, change, and possible attrition or period effects.
issues.quote: “Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.”

issues.subcategory: no demographic adjustment despite unbalanced sample
issues.description: The sample is predominantly young, female, and Pākehā, but the model does not adjust for demographic variables. Given known associations between demographics, ideology, and environmental attitudes, estimates may be confounded and are not necessarily generalizable.
issues.quote: “M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female... majority (86%) identified as Pākehā”

issues.description: The Discussion theorizes environmentalism as hierarchy-attenuating because environmental harms fall on lower-status groups. While plausible, this mechanism is not measured in the study and may not apply to the specific two-item environmental concern/exaggeration measure.
issues.quote: “environmentalism is a hierarchy-attenuating ideology: Exploitation of natural resources favours the dominant group, while the consequences fall to those at the bottom of the hierarchy.”

issues.description: The authors use prospective associations to argue that the preference for an unequal society leads to lower willingness to sacrifice. However, cross-lagged associations with annual/semester lags cannot establish the psychological process by which ideology changes environmental attitudes.
issues.quote: “The preference for an unequal society leads individuals to be less willing to make personal sacrifices for the environment.”

issues.description: The manuscript does not report institutional ethics approval, informed consent procedures, or participant protections, which are necessary for human-subjects longitudinal research.
issues.quote: “Participants and Procedure”

issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges NZAVS but does not specify whether the data used are publicly available, restricted, or how other researchers can access them. This limits reproducibility.
issues.quote: “We express our gratitude to the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS) team for their work collecting and maintaining the NZAVS.”

issues.description: The abstract says RWA was a significant negative predictor, but the magnitude is very small (B=-.02), the construct is inconsistently measured, and its unique predictive strength relative to SDO was not statistically different by the authors’ own comparison. The abstract presents a stronger and cleaner conclusion than the results support.
issues.quote: “RWA was a weaker, but significant, negative predictor.”

issues.subcategory: p-values with constrained repeated paths ambiguous
issues.description: Because paths were constrained equal across lags, each reported p-value corresponds to a single pooled/stationary parameter, not separate evidence at each time point. Some text implies effects occurred “across all time points” or “over five years” without clarifying the constrained nature of the estimate.
issues.quote: “across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time”

issues.subcategory: no assessment of nonlinear or cohort/time effects
issues.description: The stationary CLPM assumes invariant effects and does not appear to model period effects from 2009–2013, despite potential changes in political/environmental discourse. This may mask context-specific effects over the five-wave period.
issues.quote: “we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects... and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.”

issues.description: The manuscript equates RWA with desire to submit to authority/tradition, omitting authoritarian aggression despite using classic RWA items including aggressive content. This oversimplifies the construct and may misstate what aspect of RWA is related to environmental attitudes.
issues.quote: “to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority.”

issues.subcategory: study source inconsistent with NZAVS citation
issues.description: The Methods say participants were recruited through Victoria University’s introductory psychology participant pool, but then refer to the NZAVS website and thank the NZAVS team. NZAVS is a national longitudinal panel, whereas a university participant pool is not. The manuscript does not reconcile these incompatible sources.
issues.quote: “We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington.” / “Full details... are available on the NZAVS website.”
